description: We are a parent and young student team from Frisco, TX, linked to an FLL team working on water pollution. We run a neighborhood cooking-oil collection drive and study microplastics in local creeks. For Space Apps, we will use NASA Earth data to trace pollution from North Texas creeks and lakes to the Gulf of Mexico and show how the water has changed over time. We bring research and storytelling, and welcome help with data analysis and visualization.
summary:
Little drops of water make a mighty ocean, and tiny pieces of plastic can pollute one. Microplastics are now found almost everywhere, even in the human body, yet little research shows how they travel from our neighborhoods to the sea. As data centers and growing cities strain Texas water, this small problem is becoming a big one.

Aqua Ninjas, a FIRST LEGO League team from Frisco, Texas, built Earth System Trend Detective to follow that path. Satellites can't see microplastics, so our tool tracks what moves them. It uses 25 years of NASA POWER rainfall data to rank 25 Texas cities by extreme-rain trends, then maps each city's watershed to the Gulf of Mexico with NASA MODIS and VIIRS imagery. Rain carries oil and plastic from streets to creeks, lakes and the Gulf, and back into wildlife and people. Because plastics attract oily substances, we are testing whether cooking oil helps microplastics clump and travel.

Our tool turns data into action. Using Census, EPA and NREL data, a simulator estimates each city's household waste-oil potential and the drop-off sites needed to capture it. Restaurants pay for oil pickup, but homes have no option, so we run cooking-oil drives with our HOA, go door to door, and work with City of Frisco stormwater staff. Our prototype pairs a river-cleaning boat with AI that counts microplastics, and we are designing plastic capture for pools and water parks. Small Plastics. Big Mission.
details:
Earth System Trend Detective is a web tool that shows how heavy rain moves pollution through Texas's connected Earth systems, from neighborhood streets to the Gulf of Mexico. A user picks a Texas city and sees 25 years (2001–2025) of NASA POWER rainfall data, counted as extreme-rain days above 50 mm. The tool calculates each city's trend slope and p-value and ranks the cities on a leaderboard. Next, it traces the city's watershed path to the Gulf and shows NASA satellite imagery of runoff reaching the coast. Finally, it connects the data to local action. A waste-oil calculator uses U.S. Census household counts, EPA fats, oils and grease data, NREL cooking-oil estimates and North Texas Defend Your Drains results to estimate how much used cooking oil each city's homes produce. A simulator then shows how many neighborhood drop-off sites, oil drives and pool or water-park plastic traps a city would need to reach its goals.

Satellites cannot see microplastics in a creek, so our tool tracks what moves them: heavy rain that washes oil, grease and plastic down storm drains into lakes, rivers and the ocean, and back into wildlife and people. Microplastics are now found almost everywhere, even in the human body, yet little research shows how they travel from neighborhoods to the sea. Because plastics attract oily substances, we are testing whether cooking oil helps microplastics clump together and travel farther. We are collecting creek water samples and counting microplastic fragments under a microscope to build a local baseline.

The tool's benefit is that it turns complex NASA data into something a student, a family or a city leader can understand and act on. Restaurants already pay for used-oil pickup, but homes have no easy option, so household cooking oil often ends up in drains. Our team runs cooking-oil collection drives with our HOA in Frisco, does door-to-door awareness campaigns, and works with City of Frisco stormwater and environmental staff. Our intended impact is for any Texas city to use this tool to plan its own oil drop-off program and protect its water before small problems become big ones, especially as data centers and fast-growing cities put more pressure on Texas water.

The project is creative because it uses rainfall as a stand-in for a pollutant that satellites can't see, and it links global satellite data to a real kid-led community program. Our team is also building a prototype river-cleaning boat with AI that counts microplastics in water samples, and we are designing ways to capture plastic from pools and water parks before they drain.

We considered data honesty, local relevance and real-world action. Our trend results show rising extreme rain in many cities, but they are not yet statistically significant, and the tool says so clearly. Our forward lines are labeled as illustrations, not climate forecasts. Our local baseline is based on only two drives so far, and we say that too. We built a responsive, interactive web app using data from NASA POWER (MERRA-2 and GPM), MODIS, VIIRS, Landsat, PACE, the CYGNSS microplastics product and NASA Giovanni, along with U.S. Census, EPA, NREL and NCTCOG sources and our own field logs. Small Plastics. Big Mission.
